title: 356 and Counting. Deepti Sharma Is Now the Greatest Wicket-Taker in Women's International Cricket History.
excerpt: The 28-year-old all-rounder from Uttar Pradesh surpassed Jhulan Goswami's all-time record at Lord's — in the same match that ended India's T20 World Cup dream.
body:
The moment deserved a gold-framed celebration. Instead, it arrived wrapped in heartbreak.

On Sunday at Lord's, Deepti Sharma became the highest wicket-taker in the history of women's international cricket. Her 356th international scalp — Beth Mooney, caught by Smriti Mandhana in the 10th over — pushed her past the legendary Jhulan Goswami's career tally of 355 wickets across all formats. It was a milestone years in the making, achieved on the grandest stage women's cricket has ever known.

But the day belonged to Australia. Ashleigh Gardner's devastating 53 off 29 balls powered the Australians to 172/4 in reply to India's 170/4, and India's Women's T20 World Cup campaign was over. For Deepti, the record came with a bittersweet sting that only sport can deliver.

## From Agra to the History Books

Deepti Bhagwan Sharma grew up in Agra, a city better known for the Taj Mahal than for producing world-record cricketers. She bats left-handed and bowls right-arm off-break — a combination that has made her one of the most versatile all-rounders in women's cricket over the past decade.

Her career numbers are staggering. In Tests, ODIs, and T20Is combined, she has now taken more wickets than any woman who has ever played international cricket. She surpassed Goswami — the towering fast bowler who defined Indian women's cricket for two decades — not with pace but with guile, flight, and an unerring ability to take wickets in pressure moments.

Deepti had equalled the record earlier in the tournament, dismissing the Netherlands' Phebe Molkenboer for her 355th wicket. She then went wicketless against South Africa and Bangladesh, leaving the milestone tantalisingly just out of reach. It finally came in the match that mattered most — the group-stage encounter against Australia that would decide India's World Cup fate.

## A Wicket That Mattered

Harmanpreet Kaur turned to Deepti in the 10th over with Australia's chase building momentum. On the very first ball, Deepti tossed one up, tempting Mooney to go aerial. The Australian wicketkeeper-batter miscued the shot straight into Mandhana's safe hands at mid-off.

The Indian players erupted. Deepti allowed herself a brief celebration before refocusing. She knew the match was still alive. She knew the World Cup was still on the line.

It wasn't enough. Shree Charani's expensive 14th over — 16 runs conceded — swung the momentum irrevocably towards Australia. Perry and Gardner finished the chase with composure, and India's campaign ended two runs short.

## The Woman Behind the Numbers

What makes Deepti's record remarkable isn't just the volume of wickets. It's the longevity and consistency. She was part of the team that won the 2025 Women's ODI World Cup, claimed gold at the 2022 Asian Games, and lifted the 2022 Women's Asia Cup. She plays franchise cricket for UP Warriorz in the Women's Premier League and London Spirit in The Hundred, keeping her skills sharp across conditions and formats year-round.

She is not flashy. She doesn't generate the highlight-reel buzz that Harmanpreet's six-hitting or Mandhana's cover drives command. But she is the player coaches trust when the game is in the balance — the one who can bowl four tight overs in the powerplay, then come back and break a partnership in the death. Her economy rate across T20Is is among the best in the world for any spinner, male or female.

## Why NRIs Should Pay Attention

For Indian diaspora fans watching the Women's T20 World Cup from England — and many were at Lord's on Sunday, with Virat Kohli and Anushka Sharma spotted in the stands — Deepti's record is a reminder of how far Indian women's cricket has come. From an era when women's internationals drew empty stands and zero broadcast coverage, the sport now fills Lord's for a World Cup group game with India's biggest cricket stars cheering from the crowd.

Jhulan Goswami held the record for years as the symbol of that journey. Deepti Sharma now carries the torch — younger, equally relentless, and far from finished.

India's T20 World Cup may be over, but the record belongs to Deepti forever. At 28, with years of international cricket still ahead, 356 is not the end. It's a checkpoint.
